newsitem.title: UK: Chunnel wagons can burn "like blow torch"-fireman.
newsitem.headline: Chunnel wagons can burn "like blow torch"-fireman.

text.p: A British fire brigade union chief on Wednesday attacked the design of Channel Tunnel freight transporters, saying they could go off "like a blow torch" in the event of a blaze.

Services on the Anglo-French link were halted following a fire late on Monday on a freight train full of loaded trucks -- the first major accident since it opened two years ago -- and trains were still not running on Wednesday.

Fire officers have criticised the design of the rail freight transporters used to carry loaded trucks through the tunnel, focusing on their lattice-work construction, which they say is less safe than a closed wagon.
They say they issued warnings before the tunnel opened that the design -- intended to save weight -- was inherently unsafe, yet the transporters were still brought into service.

The assistant general secretary of Britain's Fire Brigades Union, Mike Fordham, attacked the design of the lorry transporters and accused the operating company, Eurotunnel SA Plc, and the British government of cutting corners to save costs.
"It is the equivalent of the design of a blowtorch," he told BBC radio.

"What I do totally object to is that Eurotunnel and the government are making decisions where they could improve the position...and they decided that the cost is too great. That is a decision that was unacceptable," he said.
The fire started on a train about 18 km (11 miles) from the French side. About 70 French and British firemen fought all night to control it.

Eurotunnel chairman Robert Malpas said "people are worrying about what went wrong when there were an awful lot of things that went right", and pointed out that passengers were evacuated to an escape tunnel which was a "haven of fresh air".
He added, however: "No transport system can be 100 percent sure and that's not a question of whether you can afford it (safety measures) or not".

A Eurotunnel spokeswoman said the design of the wagons had been approved by the Channel Tunnel Safety Authority and wagons which lacked that approval would not be used. She declined to comment on whether the design had been changed to cut costs.
Fire Brigades Union spokesman Andy Gilchrist said the lattice-style freight wagons should be replaced by a closed design, which would allow fixed fire-extinguishing systems to be installed.

The best method would be to use a system based on halon gas, which suppresses fire by depriving it of oxygen, he said. This can only be used in closed wagons, as the lattice design would allow the gas to escape.

He said present practice called for trains to be taken to the end of the tunnel for fires to be fought in the open air if possible but, with the current design of freight wagons, this could fan the flames as the train was pulled though the tunnel.
"Because the procedure is to get trains out of the tunnel, that fans and assists the fire," Gilchrist told Reuters.
He also called for the list of cargoes banned from the tunnel on fire safety grounds to be expanded.
